messages.subject: additive effects in RIL population
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Broman,

I have a RIL population with parents having early/late flowering and few QTLs were identified. Within these QTLs, only QTL 1 has negative additive effect (contribute to early flowering), while QTL 2, 3 and 4 have positive additive effects (contribute to late flowering).

My question is if we can say allele from early flowering parent on QTL 1 contribute to this negative additive effect, and vice versa? I am bit doubt about it, but remember reading something about this before...

Thank you in advance,
Susan

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] additive effects in RIL population
messages.body_plain:
A QTL with effect in the opposite direction of what you’d expect, given the parental strains’ phenotypes, is often called a “transgressive QTL”. There not unusual. The low strain will often have alleles that increase the phenotype, and the high strain will have alleles that decrease the phenotype.

karl

messages.body_plain:
In R/qtl, RIL genotypes are encoded like AA/BB, and the effects are like (ave_BB - ave_AA)/2.
So positive values indicate B allele increases the phenotype and negative values indicate A allele increases the phenotype.

karl

messages.body_plain:
To be more specific, QTL 1 is a major QTL, explaining 45% phenotypic variation, but the genotypic data from the early flowering RILs show that the allele at the QTL is from late flowering parent. Fit what you described as "transgressive QTL". However, QTL 3 only explains 6% of the phenotypic variation, and the genotypic data from the late flowering RILs or early flowering RILs have close to 50% split between the alleles from both parents. This makes it hard to call which allele play a role here.

Could you offer some suggestions/explanations for this scenario?

Thanks,
Susan

messages.body_plain:
Have a huge-effect QTL in the opposite direction is really surprising, so the first thing I'd look for is whether the effect is in the direction you think vs having the alleles swapped.

The estimated effects of the identified QTL won't generally add up to the observed difference between the parents, both because the estimated effects are subject to selection bias, and there will be many additional loci that haven't been identified.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

Recently, I've been working on a QTL analysis with the R/QTL package in a tomato RIL population.

I performed several steps of analysis:
1. Scanone, which revealed 3 QTLs.
2. Scantwo: which shows that between two of the QTLs also found in scanone, there is an additive effect (significant LOD scores for full, fv1, av1 and add, but not for int).
See the table below (due to the confidentiality of my project I'm afraid I can't share the chromosomes and positions, but I can say the 2 additive QTLs are on separate chromosomes)

               pos1f pos2f lod.full lod.fv1 lod.int <http://lod.int>     pos1a pos2a lod.add lod.av1
chr.A:chr. B                 8.99    5.64    1.12                    7.87    4.53

Scantwo "imp", 1000 permutations
   full  fv1  int  add  av1  one
1% 6.87 5.59 4.88 5.67 3.93 3.52
5% 6.08 4.53 3.98 4.92 3.13 2.82

3. StepwiseQTL, which also selects the model with the three QTLs found in the other analyses.

However, when I make an effectplot for the two QTLs (the ones on chr. A and chr. B) that show up as additive in scantwo, I do not see a significant additive effect of the QTLs, as the errobars overlap at: see the picture below.
I also performed an ANOVA to test for significant differences between the RILs with the 4 different allele combinations. This ANOVA confirms the effect of the individual QTLs, but finds no evidence for an addititve effect.

Thus it seems like the scantwo tells me that there is an additive effect, while the effectplot tells me there is no evidence for an additive effect.

Thus, I am wondering, which data/analysis is the most trustworthy? The scantwo, or the inspection of the effectplot?
What do you think?

Thanks!

Best wishes,
Jasper

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Interpretation of scantwo additive effects
messages.body_plain:
It sounds to me like the results all support the conclusion: there are three QTL, and they act additively (no epistasis).

To say QTL act additively means the effect of one QTL is not dependent on the genotype at another. This corresponds to having parallel lines in the effect plot.

I find scantwo most useful for identifying potential interactions among QTL, and for determining if there may be multiple QTL on a single chromosome. The results you're getting say that adjusting for the locus on chr.A, there's evidence for a QTL on chr.B, and vice versa.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] pseudo test cross strategy
messages.body_plain:
As I understand the pseudo test cross, you've done a cross between two outbred individuals, but then are focusing only on markers segregating in one of the two parents. In this case, the genotypes in the offspring are as in a backcross. If I were to use this approach, I would format the data like a backcross, with genotypes say AA and AB.

The ideal treatment of a cross between outbreds in R/qtl would be as a phase-known four-way cross (cross type "4way"). But you would need to infer the phase (in other words, the haplotypes) in the two parents, which would ideally be done with genotype data on the four grandparents. In this case, genotypes have to be coded in a somewhat complicated way, with integers 1-14. Assuming the two parents' chromosomes are labeled AB x CD, the codes are described in the help file for read.cross:

NA = missing, 1 = AC, 2 = BC, 3 = AD, 4 = BD, 5 = A = AC or AD, 6 = B = BC or BD, 7 = C = AC or BC, 8 = D = AD or BD, 9 = AC or BD, 10 = AD or BC, 11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD

karl

Also, since in forming linkage groups you end up with one block that has the vast majority of the markers, it seems you should reduce the max.rf and increase the min.lod in the call to formLinkageGroups.

But if you have a physical map, I don't understand why you would try to construct a linkage map from scratch. The physical map would tell you what chromosomes the markers are on, as well as their order along the chromosome.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,
I've inherited a QTL project for a RIL population as well as some code from a colleague, and I am a QTL beginner. I'm wondering if the following depiction of a QTL is acceptable:

The code follows this general pattern:
1) run scanone on trait A
2) run effectscan on trait A
3) take the absolute value of the additive effect from the effectscan apply this to the scanone LOD score (code below if I am not explaining it clearly)
4) plot the modified scanone results so that the QTL is either positive or negative, according to the results of the effect scan

effscan.traitA <- effectscan(sim.geno(DATA),pheno.col = 6, draw = FALSE)

#run scanone
IM.traitA <- scanone(DATA,pheno.col=6)

# change the "allelic" direction of the LOD score by dividing the effect by the absolute value of the effect, we get 1 or -1
#then multiply the LOD score from scanone by that and you get a directed LOD score
IM.traitA[,3] = IM.traitA[,3] * effscan.traitA[,3]/abs(effscan.traitA[,3])

Then we repeat this for trait B. When we plot both of their modified scanone results together, it looks like this:

We are very interested in what's going on in chromosome 2, which is why my colleague liked this depiction of the QTLs. I am wondering if this is an ok way to show our results. From reading the R/qtl book, it seems like you can either show the standard scanone result OR the figure generated by effectscan. Is it ok to combine the two?

Thank you very much!

In the first instance, pheno.col=1:5 should be valid, provided that you have at least 5 phenotypes.

In the second instance, you need to combine the multiple phenotype names into a vector using c().

    mydata.scan1<- scanone(mydata_reduced,pheno.col = c("PH","SD","DTF","Biomass","brix"), method = "em")

messages.subject: model selection
messages.body_plain:
I have a RIL population of 170 lines that was genotyped with GBS (N=5,663) and KASP (N=18) SNPs. I have run several different QTL models and am unsure whether I have one QTL or two QTL right next to each other. I have run:
1. scanone and addqtl up to a max of seven QTLs
2. stepwiseqtl, "imp" 1k permutation of scantwo for penalties, default of max 10 qtl
3. stepwiseqtl, same settings except max of 3 qtl
4. stepwiseqtl, max of 2
5. stepwiseqtl, max of 1
The LOD profile plots of each are attached. Each model gives a different number of significant QTL. What would be the most appropriate model for this situation? Sample scripts are provided below.

scanone script:
for(pht in names)
{
form1<-"y ~ Q1"
scan1<-scanone(x, pheno.col=pht, method="imp", model="normal")
print(pht)
print(maxS1<-max(scan1))
scan1chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS1$chr))
qtl1<-makeqtl(x, chr=scan1chr, pos=maxS1$pos, what="draws")

form2 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2"
scan2<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = qtl1, formula= form2, method="imp", model="normal")
maxS2<-max(scan2)
scan2chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS2$chr))
qtl2<-makeqtl(x, chr=c(scan1chr,scan2chr), pos=c(maxS1$pos,maxS2$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref2 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form2, qtl=qtl2, method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl2, formula=form2, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

form3 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3"
scan3<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref2, formula= form3, method="imp", model="normal")
maxS3<-max(scan3)
scan3chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS3$chr))
qtl3<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref2$chr,scan3chr),pos=c(ref2$pos,maxS3$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref3 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form3, qtl=qtl3, method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl3, formula=form3, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

form4 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4"
scan4<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref3, formula= form4,method="imp", model="normal")
maxS4<-max(scan4)
scan4chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS4$chr))
qtl4<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref3$chr,scan4chr),pos=c(ref3$pos,maxS4$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref4 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form4, qtl=qtl4,method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl4, formula=form4, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

form5 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5"
scan5<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref4, formula= form5,method="imp", model="normal")
maxS5<-max(scan5)
scan5chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS5$chr))
qtl5<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref4$chr,scan5chr),pos=c(ref4$pos,maxS5$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref5 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form5, qtl=qtl5,method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl5, formula=form5, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

form6 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5+ Q6"
scan6<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref5, formula= form6,method="imp", model="normal")
maxS6<-max(scan6)
scan6chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS6$chr))
qtl6<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref5$chr,scan6chr),pos=c(ref5$pos,maxS6$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref6 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form6, qtl=qtl6,method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl6, formula=form6, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

form7 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5 + Q6 + Q7"
scan7<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref6, formula= form7,method="imp", model="normal")
maxS7<-max(scan7)
scan7chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS7$chr))
qtl7<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref6$chr,scan7chr),pos=c(ref6$pos,maxS7$pos), what="draws")
print(summary(ref7 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form7, qtl=qtl7,method="imp", model="normal")))
print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl7, formula=form7, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))

image<-paste("quickQTLimp",pht,".svg",sep="")
svg(image)
plot(scan1,col="black", main=pht)
plot(scan2, add=T, col="red")
plot(scan3, add=T, col="blue")
plot(scan4, add=T, col="green")
plot(scan5, add=T, col="orange")
plot(scan6, add=T, col="magenta")
plot(scan7, add=T, col="gray")

Stepwiseqtl script
print(pens<-calc.penalties(perms, alpha=.05))
step<-stepwiseqtl(x, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", max.qtl=5,
penalties=pens,additive.only=FALSE, refine.locations=TRUE,keeptrace=TRUE, keeplodprofile=TRUE)
summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=step, formula=formula(step), pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T))

messages.body_plain:
In general, I would recommend to use the penalized LOD score to help decide on the support for the different models.
scanone() followed by repeated calls to addqtl() is effectively the same as what is done in stepwiseqtl(), but stepwiseqtl() just produces the single model with largest penalized LOD score.

I guess I'd focus on that larger model and the look particularly at the relative support for adding or removing a locus on chromosome 9.

I would also pay attention to which of your 170 lines are actually showing recombination events between the inferred QTL. It is the lines with recombination events in the region that are providing the evidence for there being a single versus multiple QTL in the region.

karl

On Thursday, May 28, 2020 at 11:37:17 AM UTC-4, Karl Broman wrote:

> In general, I would recommend to use the penalized LOD score to help decide on the support for the different models.
> scanone() followed by repeated calls to addqtl() is effectively the same as what is done in stepwiseqtl(), but stepwiseqtl() just produces the single model with largest penalized LOD score.
>
> I guess I'd focus on that larger model and the look particularly at the relative support for adding or removing a locus on chromosome 9.
>
> I would also pay attention to which of your 170 lines are actually showing recombination events between the inferred QTL. It is the lines with recombination events in the region that are providing the evidence for there being a single versus multiple QTL in the region.
>
> karl
>

> On Thu, May 28, 2020 at 8:54 AM Sandra Pelc <sandr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I have a RIL population of 170 lines that was genotyped with GBS (N=5,663) and KASP (N=18) SNPs. I have run several different QTL models and am unsure whether I have one QTL or two QTL right next to each other. I have run:
> > 1. scanone and addqtl up to a max of seven QTLs
> > 2. stepwiseqtl, "imp" 1k permutation of scantwo for penalties, default of max 10 qtl
> > 3. stepwiseqtl, same settings except max of 3 qtl
> > 4. stepwiseqtl, max of 2
> > 5. stepwiseqtl, max of 1
> > The LOD profile plots of each are attached. Each model gives a different number of significant QTL. What would be the most appropriate model for this situation? Sample scripts are provided below.
> >
> > scanone script:
> > for(pht in names)
> > {
> > form1<-"y ~ Q1"
> > scan1<-scanone(x, pheno.col=pht, method="imp", model="normal")
> > print(pht)
> > print(maxS1<-max(scan1))
> > scan1chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS1$chr))
> > qtl1<-makeqtl(x, chr=scan1chr, pos=maxS1$pos, what="draws")
> >
> > form2 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2"
> > scan2<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = qtl1, formula= form2, method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS2<-max(scan2)
> > scan2chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS2$chr))
> > qtl2<-makeqtl(x, chr=c(scan1chr,scan2chr), pos=c(maxS1$pos,maxS2$pos), what="draws")
> > print(summary(ref2 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form2, qtl=qtl2, method="imp", model="normal")))
> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl2, formula=form2, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
> >
> > form3 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3"
> > scan3<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref2, formula= form3, method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS3<-max(scan3)
> > scan3chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS3$chr))
> > qtl3<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref2$chr,scan3chr),pos=c(ref2$pos,maxS3$pos), what="draws")
> > print(summary(ref3 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form3, qtl=qtl3, method="imp", model="normal")))
> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl3, formula=form3, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
> >
> > form4 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4"
> > scan4<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref3, formula= form4,method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS4<-max(scan4)
> > scan4chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS4$chr))
> > qtl4<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref3$chr,scan4chr),pos=c(ref3$pos,maxS4$pos), what="draws")
> > print(summary(ref4 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form4, qtl=qtl4,method="imp", model="normal")))
> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl4, formula=form4, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
> >
> > form5 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5"
> > scan5<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref4, formula= form5,method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS5<-max(scan5)
> > scan5chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS5$chr))
> > qtl5<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref4$chr,scan5chr),pos=c(ref4$pos,maxS5$pos), what="draws")
> > print(summary(ref5 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form5, qtl=qtl5,method="imp", model="normal")))
> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl5, formula=form5, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
> >
> > form6 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5+ Q6"
> > scan6<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref5, formula= form6,method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS6<-max(scan6)
> > scan6chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS6$chr))
> > qtl6<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref5$chr,scan6chr),pos=c(ref5$pos,maxS6$pos), what="draws")
> > print(summary(ref6 <- refineqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, formula = form6, qtl=qtl6,method="imp", model="normal")))
> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl6, formula=form6, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
> >
> > form7 <- "y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5 + Q6 + Q7"
> > scan7<-addqtl(x, pheno.col = pht, qtl = ref6, formula= form7,method="imp", model="normal")
> > maxS7<-max(scan7)
> > scan7chr<-as.numeric(as.character(maxS7$chr))
> > qtl7<-makeqtl(x,chr=c(ref6$chr,scan7chr),pos=c(ref6$pos,maxS7$pos), what="draws")

> > print(summary(fitqtl(x, qtl=qtl7, formula=form7, pheno.col=pht,method="imp", model="normal", get.ests=T, dropone=T)))
